name: Mansa Musa
intro: You are Musa, mansa (king of kings) of Mali, the richest realm in West Africa: its gold fields at Bambuk and Bure supply much of the gold that reaches the Mediterranean. You are a Muslim ruler over many subjects who are not. It is 1324 and you have decided to make the pilgrimage to Mecca.

sources.cite: Al-Umari, Masalik al-absar fi mamalik al-amsar (c. 1337-38), in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-Ibar, in Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus (1981)
Michael A. Gomez, African Dominion: A New History of Empire in Early and Medieval West Africa (2018)

at.n: Mali, the royal capital (site debated; Niani shown)

chapters.title: The pilgrimage
chapters.text: A pilgrim king is a statement: Mali is a Muslim power to be reckoned with in Cairo and Mecca. Arab writers will later say thousands went with you and that you carried tons of gold; the exact numbers are not trustworthy.

choices.t: Go in full state, with a great caravan and gold
choices.out: You cross the Sahara by way of Walata and Tuat. Your caravan is remembered for centuries.

choices.t: Go quietly, as a simple pilgrim
choices.out: Mali stays a rumour to the Mediterranean world. No Catalan mapmaker draws you holding a nugget of gold.

choices.t: Stay home and send an envoy
choices.out: Mansas before you had gone, and your authority rests partly on Islam's prestige. Staying keeps you safer but smaller.
choices.end: A ruler known only from oral tradition in Mali.

chapters.took: Mali to Cairo across the Sahara: arrived July 1324. Sahara crossings with a big caravan took about two to three months of travel.
chapters.title: Kiss the ground?
chapters.text: Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad receives you. Court officials tell you to kiss the ground before him, as everyone does.

choices.out: Al-Umari's informants say you hesitated, then said you would bow to God who created you, and did so. The sultan seats you beside him and gives you robes and a horse.

choices.t: Kiss the ground like any vassal
choices.out: Easier, but it says Mali is a client of Egypt. Your prestige at home suffers.

chapters.title: Rivers of gold
chapters.text: Your people spend and give gold freely in Cairo's markets.

choices.out: Al-Umari, writing about twelve years later, says so much gold came in that its value in Cairo fell and had still not recovered.

choices.t: Keep your gold for the road home
choices.out: You return solvent. But the legend that put you on maps and in headlines 700 years later is never born.

chapters.title: Bringing the world home
chapters.text: After the hajj, you can bring scholars, books and builders back to Mali. Al-Sahili, a poet and scholar from Granada, is in Mecca.

choices.t: Recruit scholars and al-Sahili to come home with you
choices.out: Al-Sahili comes to Mali. Later tradition credits him with an audience hall at the capital and with the Djinguereber mosque at Timbuktu.

choices.t: Buy books, but bring no one
choices.out: Books without teachers do less. Timbuktu's rise as a city of scholars might have come slower.

chapters.title: Out of money
chapters.text: On the way back your gold has run out. Cairo's merchants will lend, at a price.

choices.t: Borrow from Cairo's merchants at high interest
choices.out: You borrow heavily. Some lenders are repaid later in Mali; Ibn Khaldun and al-Umari tell stories of creditors who travelled to collect.

choices.t: Sell what you have and go home lighter
choices.out: No debts, but some of your retinue is lost or left behind.

chapters.title: City of learning
chapters.text: Gao, on the Niger, has come under Mali's rule (the timing is uncertain; traditions credit your general Saghmandia). You pass through on the way home and can build in Timbuktu.

choices.t: Build a great mosque at Timbuktu
choices.out: The Djinguereber mosque is built of earth and wood around 1327. Rebuilt many times, it still stands and is a World Heritage site.

choices.t: Spend it on the army instead
choices.out: Mali's power did rest on its cavalry. But the mosque and Timbuktu's scholars are what the world remembers.

epilogue: Musa died around 1337. In 1375 the Catalan Atlas showed a West African king on a throne holding a gold nugget, labelled as the richest and noblest king in the land. Within a century of his death Mali was shrinking, and Songhay, centred on Gao, took its place.
